frontMatter.title: The Great Language Smackdown: 104 Languages Through Three Lenses

frontMatterLines: title: "The Great Language Smackdown: 104 Languages Through Three Lenses"

blocks.p: **Analysis date: October 2026. Later general-availability releases are added as they ship and state their own date: TypeScript 7.0 (8 July 2026), Dart 3.13 (12 August 2026), Go 1.27 (19 August 2026), Java 27 (15 September 2026), Rust 1.99 (1 October 2026), and Gleam 1.19 (5 October 2026). Two new families joined in October 2026. Goose (v2026.3, released 21 October 2026), a language whose repository was first published on 28 August 2026 and which sits outside the TIOBE top 50, is assessed against its own release date. So is G# (0.5.212, released 22 October 2026), a .NET language by David Obando whose repository dates to 2019-05-22, sat dormant from 2023-05-19 to 2026-05-17, and has released from v0.1.270 (2026-05-29) on a self-hosted compiler since v0.5.3; it too is assessed against its own release date. Three further families are assessed at a historical release beside their current one: C++98, C++11, and C++23; JavaScript ES5, ES2015, and ES2025; and Python 2.7 with Python 3.14. The older snapshot records the release of its era and states the constructs it did not have; the family's current page assesses the release named there. The Java line is assessed release by release, from 1.4 through 27: the language releases move the mechanisms, and the runtime-only releases (6, 26, 27) record what changed without moving them. Every other language is evaluated against its latest stable version as of the October 2026 date. The TIOBE top 50 is covered as of October 2026.**

Most language comparisons rank languages on **adoption, adoption rate, and the feature list**. Adoption counts the teams that chose a language. Adoption rate counts how fast that number moves. The feature list counts what a language offers the people who write in it. All three read the language from the side that gains: how many people want it, how quickly that group grows, and how much the language gives them.

This analysis reads the same 104 languages from the side that pays. It asks what a language **brings with it when it is used**: the agreements the code must keep, the shared resources the code must reach through, and the readiness gaps it leaves in the artifact. Each agreement a mechanism names is charged when it is present. Two facts are recorded and priced nothing: a mechanism whose direction the model cannot fix (`V5`), and a crossing delivery target whose promise no document decides.

The inversion is deliberate. Adoption and features are the language's gain. The costs this analysis prices fall on the people who keep the code, and a popularity number does not price them: a demand count says how many teams chose the language, not what the code asks of the people who keep it.

**Coupling is the cost that propagates, and accidental coupling is the part of it no requirement asked for.** Coupling is access to a shared resource: when the producer of that resource changes, every consumer moves with it. The [coupling analysis](../coupling/index.qmd) sets a floor — the shared-resource edges the system genuinely needs — and calls every edge above it a boundary defect or an accidental edge. Necessary coupling is made visible and governed. Accidental coupling is removed. The page develops the distinction below, in [A coupling taxonomy: accidental vs. necessary](#a-coupling-taxonomy-accidental-vs.-necessary): the accidental kind splits into the coupling a better design removes and the coupling only the language's own constructs impose. The **Core coupling** axis prices the part of that list the language imposes: the agreements its own constructs force into ordinary code. The inventory names 43 of them, and an agreement the inventory does not name is not priced.

rawtable: | The usual yardstick | What it measures | What it cannot see |
| Adoption count | How many teams chose the language | What those teams' maintainers pay |
| Adoption rate | How fast adoption is moving | Whether the code is easy to change later |
| Feature list | What the language offers | What the language imposes |
| Benchmark result | What a program costs to run | What a program costs to change |

blocks.p: The model prices a different question: which named agreements a language forces on the code written in it, and which readiness gaps it leaves in the artifact. Its inventory of 99 mechanisms contains no features: the score removes points for a harm that is present, and pays nothing for a language being good at anything. What a change will cost a program, and whether its code is easy to change, stay outside the score.

This analysis examines each language on **three scored axes** — **Core coupling** (how much accidental coupling do the language's own constructs force?), **Ecosystem coupling** (what do the platform, the tooling, and the release packaging cost?), and **engineering readiness** (can you rebuild the artifact, verify what you shipped, observe it, work in it quickly, connect it to other languages, and count on its governance?) — plus one unscored **profile** (what does it cost to run, how well do coding models and agents work in it, and is there a safety-certified path?).

rawtable: | **Core coupling** | How much accidental coupling does the language force into the code itself? |
| **Ecosystem coupling** | What does the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost? |
| **Engineering readiness** | Can the artifact be rebuilt, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected, and governed? |
| **Profile** (unscored) | What does it cost to run, how well do coding models work in it, and is there a safety-certified path? |

blocks.q: **Version scope**: Every language is assessed against its **latest stable standard or release** as of the analysis date stated above — October 2026 for the set as a whole, September 2026 for Java 27 [@isoC2024; @isoCpp2024; @isoAda2023; @isoFortran2023; @isoCobol2023; @ecmaEiffel; @isoSql2023; @posix2024; @r7rs2013; @ansiSmalltalk1998]. Scores reflect modern idioms and current best practices for that version, not historical usage. Where a language has multiple widely-used versions with meaningfully different coupling properties, this is noted explicitly.

**Scope.** This is a **language analysis with two scores and an unscored profile** — coupling and engineering readiness, plus a profile — a topic distinct from the Independent Variation Principle (IVP). The coupling score measures how much *language-imposed coupling* each language inflicts on programs; the readiness score measures whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly. **None of the three** identifies change drivers, computes driver assignments, or measures module cohesion; those belong to IVP and are outside this analysis. Each language has its own page with the full detailed evaluation; the sections below give the grouped results and rankings.

blocks.p: The language exists to control memory and hardware directly: a runtime is optional, and layout is the programmer's business.
The language's main business is building general application software, with a managed runtime or a rich standard library.
The language's centre of gravity is the browser or the HTTP request and response model.
The language's primary object is a dataset or a numeric array, not a program loop.

The language's work is to drive a system: issuing commands, processing text streams, and gluing other programs together. Some members are interactive command interpreters; Perl is not, and belongs by the work, not the mechanism.
The language targets bare hardware, fixed timing, or a certification regime for a safety-critical system.
The language's purpose is to make a machine check a claim about a program.
The language is retained for systems already written in it; new work in it is the exception.
The language exists mainly to teach programming.
The language compiles to a chain's execution model.

ul: **Need maximum safety?** → Rust, SPARK, Lean 4, Rocq, PureScript, Haskell, Ada
**Formal verification?** → SPARK, Lean 4, Rocq (theorem provers)
**Building enterprise apps?** → C#, Java, Kotlin, TypeScript
**Web development?** → TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Ruby, PHP
**Systems programming?** → Rust, C, D, Zig, C++
**Data science/ML?** → Python, R, Julia, MATLAB, SQL
**Scripting/automation?** → Python, Bash, Zsh, Fish, PowerShell, Lua
**Learning programming?** → Scratch, Python, JavaScript, Scheme
**Functional programming?** → Haskell, OCaml, Elixir, F#, Clojure, Scheme, PureScript, Unison
**Game development?** → C++, C#, Rust, D, Lua (scripting)
**Mobile apps?** → Swift (iOS), Kotlin (Android), Dart (Flutter), C# (.NET MAUI)
**Fault-tolerant distributed?** → Erlang, Elixir (BEAM/OTP)
**Cross-platform UI?** → Dart (Flutter), Kotlin (Compose Multiplatform)
**Scientific/numerical?** → Julia, Python, R, MATLAB, Fortran

blocks.text: A coupling taxonomy: accidental vs. necessary

blocks.p: Coupling falls into two fundamental kinds:

rawtable: | **Necessary coupling** | Dependencies the system cannot function without — its *irreducible coupling floor*. The floor is a property of the system and its domain, never of the language, and no score in this analysis measures a distance to it. | Domain artifacts |
| **Accidental coupling** | Dependencies that are not causally required — coupling that exists by developer choice, oversight, or language/platform constraint. | Design or platform |

blocks.p: In any system, necessary coupling is the minimum possible: the inter-module communication the domain demands. Accidental coupling is everything beyond that — coupling introduced by design choice, oversight, or the language and platform itself. This taxonomy, and the coupling-floor idea it rests on, is developed in the coupling analysis: the definition of coupling as access to a shared resource [@loth2026couplingnature], and the coupling floor as the coupling the domain demands [@loth2026couplingconsequence].
Accidental coupling subdivides into two subtypes, which are the core of this language analysis:

rawtable: | **Avoidable accidental** | Could be removed by better design within the language's capabilities. The developer chose to couple unnecessarily. | Better design |

| **Language-imposed** | Unavoidable given the language's constructs — the irreducible residuum of accidental coupling the language *inflicts* on all programs. Even optimal design cannot eliminate it. | Change language or version |

blocks.p: A language can also couple elements in dimensions beyond structural dependency. Coupling has several dimensions: structural, temporal, concurrency, security, platform, and **language** (memory model, type system, module system). Each dimension carries its own dependency relation, and coupling decomposes into necessary and accidental components.

**What this means for language comparison:** This article evaluates languages along the *language* coupling dimension: how much language-imposed coupling does the language generate, and how well does it help you detect and eliminate avoidable accidental coupling? A language with a good coupling profile (a) minimizes language-imposed coupling (fewer constructs that force accidental edges) and (b) detects avoidable coupling at the earliest possible stage (compile time > static analysis > runtime > never).

The **coupling scores** answer: *how much agreement does this language force on the code written in it?* The **readiness score** answers a separate question, stated with it below. The **profile** is not scored. The **ranking score** is coupling, lifted by at most 15% for readiness — coupling is primary, because the code is what remains and readiness is remediable by process. The rule is stated on [the Scoring Model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd).

blocks.text: How the Scores Are Computed: Methodology

blocks.p: Every language imposes some amount of accidental coupling that even optimal design cannot eliminate. Headers force compilation coupling. Unchecked null forces null-check coupling. A global interpreter lock forces concurrency coupling. Dynamic typing forces coupling detection to runtime. These are not design mistakes — they are language properties.
The scores in this analysis are computed by a **fixed, mechanical rule**, not by subjective impression:

ol: 1. A **closed mechanism inventory** — each coupling mechanism has a **fixed weight**.
2. A **binary presence check** — for each language, each mechanism is marked *present* or *absent* (a factual determination, not a severity judgment).
3. An **arithmetic rule** — the present weights are summed, and the axis score is **100 × (1 − present weight ÷ inventory weight)**, the share of the axis inventory the language forces.

blocks.p: Because the weights are fixed and the only per-language step is present/absent, any two analysts following these rules reach identical scores. The framework makes disagreement precise: to dispute a score, you must either contest a mechanism's presence in a specific language, or propose changing a fixed weight and then recompute.

**The full mechanism inventory** (Core coupling: Type, Construction, Memory, Error, Concurrency, Platform; Ecosystem coupling: Performance, Ecosystem, Evolution, Domain, Learning, Syntax, Testing, Security; Engineering readiness: Reproducibility, Supply chain, Observability, Feedback, Interop, Governance), the detailed severity-share rule, and the tests that decide presence are on [The Scoring Model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd). The ranked tables, the per-dimension sub-scores, and the **complete per-language mechanism-presence data** for all 104 languages — so any score can be reproduced from first principles — are on [The Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd).

**What each mechanism means** — what it is, what it forces to agree, how harmful it is, and why it removes the points it removes — is explained mechanism by mechanism, with examples, in [the Criteria](scoring-criteria.qmd).

**Three scores, not one.** The comparison reports **Core coupling** (what the language's own constructs force), **Ecosystem coupling** (what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost), and **Engineering readiness** (whether the artifact can be rebuilt, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to another language, and governed openly). The three scores are reported separately and are never summed. They are correlated in practice — a missing package registry affects both Ecosystem coupling and the supply chain — but each is scored on its own axis. Alongside them, an unscored **profile** records three axes a score cannot price — energy and cost, AI and agent readiness, and safety certification — language by language.
Because the model is a fixed inventory scored by severity share, the bands are thresholds over that share:

ul: **90+**: under 10 points of cost — on Core, under 36 raw weight, usually in one dimension.
**75–89**: 10 to 25 points — on Core, 36 to 88 raw weight, across a few dimensions.
**60–74**: 25 to 40 points — on Core, 88 to 140 raw weight.
**45–59**: 40 to 55 points — on Core, 140 to 192 raw weight.

**below 45**: over 55 points of cost — on Core, over 192 raw weight; five or six dimensions carry a priced mechanism, and at least four reach 15 in raw weight. The language's design trades separation of concerns for other goals (simplicity, flexibility, ubiquity, or direct hardware access).

blocks.p: **Five snapshots reach the 90+ band today** — Rocq 95.7, Unison 95.4, Lean 4 94.6, Haskell 92.0, and Gleam 90.9. Rust 1.96 and Rust 1.99 sit at 89.7, PureScript at 88.9, and SPARK at 85.4, just below. None reaches 100: every language carries at least one priced mechanism, and the gap to 100 is the progression margin left to language design.

The readiness score uses the same arithmetic over its six dimensions, the same three tiers, and the same bands. Every readiness mechanism is priced by breadth, escape, and silence exactly as a coupling mechanism is: a readiness gap that runs across the whole artifact, that the team cannot close locally, and that nothing in the language records is High. Its inventory therefore totals 171 points, and its scores move in the same fractional steps as Core. A readiness band is still not comparable to a coupling band, because the two axes price different kinds of cost. The readiness bands are listed with the coupling bands under “By Score” below, and on the [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd).
Every score in the comparison — the ranked table, the three per-dimension matrices, and the complete per-language mechanism data — is on the [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd).
**By Paradigm:**

ul: **Type System Powerhouses** → Maximum safety, steep learning curves
**Modern Mainstream** → Best balance for most projects
**Systems and Performance** → When you need low-level control
**Dynamic and Scripting** → Rapid prototyping, flexibility over safety
**Domain-Specific** → Perfect fit for specialized problems

blocks.p: **By Score (latest version, modern idioms):**

*Ranked by Core coupling from the model (severity share per axis); the numbers behind every grouping below are on the [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd). Analysis date October 2026 — older versions of the same language can score significantly lower (e.g., C++98, Java 8).*
**If you need mathematical proof of correctness:** Rocq, SPARK, Lean 4
**If you want bulletproof low coupling by language design:** Unison, Rocq, Rust, SQL
**If you want low coupling with pragmatism:** Haskell, PureScript, Zig, OCaml
**If you want low coupling with discipline (modern versions):** Elixir, Erlang, Clojure, Transact-SQL, Dart, Kotlin, Delphi, Go
**Low coupling on a budget (ecosystem-driven):** Tcl, F#, Scala, C++

**Specialized excellence (unique coupling profiles):** Erlang: Actor model with per-process isolation and let-it-crash. Elixir: Modern BEAM with macros and protocols. Julia: Multiple dispatch without inheritance. Eiffel: Design by Contract states each routine's obligations in the source. Objective-C: Dynamic messaging plus categories, protocols, and blocks for decoupling. Turbo Pascal: Units give genuine interface/implementation separation rare among 1980s languages.

**Domain-locked procedural database logic:** PL/SQL, PL/pgSQL, SQL PL, SAP ASE, and Transact-SQL couple all logic to their database engines but offer real encapsulation (packages, modules, stored procedures). Structured exceptions are the norm, but SAP ASE's Transact-SQL dialect carries no `TRY ... CATCH`, so its failure path is `@@error` checks. SAS uniquely separates the DATA step from PROC steps. Use them only where the logic must live inside the database or analytics engine.
**Lowest forced coupling:**

ol: 1. **Rocq**: Machine-checked proof as the unit of development
2. **Unison**: Content-addressed code, algebraic effects, distributed computing built-in
3. **Rust**: Ownership enforces separation, Result types compose, no null, traits decouple
4. **Lean 4**: Dependent types over a small trusted kernel
5. **SPARK**: A proved Ada subset, so the proof is part of the build

blocks.p: **Low coupling with pragmatism (latest versions):**

ol: 3. **Zig**: Explicit everything, error unions, allocator parameters, comptime
4. **OCaml**: Module system, immutable data, exhaustive pattern matching

blocks.p: **Highest forced coupling:**

ol: 1. **Assembly**: No abstractions, manual everything, maximum coupling risk
2. **C**: Manual memory, weak typing, global state, undefined behavior
3. **Perl**: Dynamic, global state, primitive objects, GIL
4. **JavaScript**: Dynamic, global state, unchecked errors, no types
6. **PHP**: Dynamic, weak typing, superglobals, no concurrency
7. **TypeScript**: JavaScript's runtime coupling under a compile-time type layer

blocks.p: **Neither helps nor hinders coupling:**

ul: **C**: With discipline, coupling can be low; without it, coupling is extreme
**D**: Better C++ with cleaner templates, contracts, and both GC and manual memory

blocks.p: Coupling scores depend heavily on which version of a language you're using. C++23 is a fundamentally different language from C++98. Java 26 with records, sealed classes, and virtual threads is not the same as Java 8. Always check the version baseline.
Version aside, Coupling scores don't determine project success. Context matters:

ul: **Team expertise** trumps language coupling score
**Ecosystem maturity** often beats language elegance
**Hiring availability** is a real constraint
**Performance requirements** eliminate choices
**Platform constraints** narrow the field

blocks.p: **But here's what coupling analysis reveals:**
Languages with **proven separation** (Lean 4, Rocq, SPARK) let a machine check a claim against a stated specification. The remaining risk moves to the specification, and the learning curve is steep.
Languages with **enforced separation** (Rust, Haskell, PureScript, OCaml) make coupling impossible to hide. You pay upfront in learning curve, gain long-term in maintainability.
Languages with **optional separation** (Swift, Kotlin, C#, modern Java, modern C++, Eiffel, Groovy) let you choose coupling level. Good for migration, requires discipline.

Languages with **manual separation** (C, D, Zig, COBOL, Turbo Pascal) put the separation burden on the programmer: the same language supports a carefully separated design and a tangled one. Expertise required.

Languages with **runtime-only separation** (JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Ruby, shells, VBScript) defer most coupling detection to testing. TypeScript moves a share of that detection to compile time, but its runtime coupling is JavaScript's. Python 3.14 (free-threaded), PHP 8.4 (property hooks, fibers), and Ruby 4.0 (YJIT, pattern matching) have all made meaningful coupling-separation progress in recent versions.

Languages with **domain-locked separation** (Objective-C, PL/SQL, Transact-SQL, SAS, Solidity) are coupled to a single platform or domain — the platform is the unit boundary, and the language's coupling quality only matters within it.

**One result worth stating plainly:** the type layer now moves the number. TypeScript scores above JavaScript, because the type layer removes `T1`, `T4`, `T5`, and `T10` and leaves `T7`: JavaScript carries `T1`, `T3`, `T4`, `T5`, `T10`, `T12`, `T13`, and `T14`; TypeScript carries `T3`, `T7`, `T12`, `T13`, and `T14`. JavaScript carries 59 Type severity points against TypeScript’s 40 — 19 raw points, worth 5.4 Core points — and TypeScript also drops `M3`, so the two snapshots sit 8.9 Core points apart: 54.0 against 62.9. The presence lists still carry the detail.

**The lesson:** Match language coupling capabilities to your context AND your version. C++23 with modern idioms is a different beast from C++98. Java 26 with virtual threads, records, and sealed classes is not Java 8. Don't pick a language based on its worst version. Building life-critical systems? Use SPARK or Lean 4. Building a 20-year system with changing requirements? Invest in Rust. Building mobile apps? Swift or Kotlin. Building a weekend project? JavaScript is fine. Maintaining legacy code? TypeScript adds compile-time detection incrementally, though its runtime coupling is JavaScript's. Need shell automation? PowerShell adds objects, Fish adds interactive polish, and Bash stays the portable default.
No language is best in every context. The scores show where a language matches your constraints and where it will charge you; design covers the rest.
The evidence points away from a single winner: different contexts need different coupling trade-offs, and the scores price them.
The scores are a starting point. The design work is yours.
The coupling account this analysis rests on is developed in the published coupling papers:

ul: *On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access* [@loth2026couplingnature] defines coupling as access to a shared resource, with the resource taxonomy and the three coupling modes.
*A Self-Contained Derivation of the Optimal Modularization from Coupling* [@loth2026couplingderivation] derives the modularisation directive from the coupling account alone.

*Coupling as a Consequence of Cohesion: Decomposition, the Coupling Floor, and Domain-Imposed Coupling* [@loth2026couplingconsequence] establishes the coupling floor and shows that correctly bounded coupling is a consequence of cohesion.

blocks.p: The link to knowledge — why a language that scatters or hides a module's knowledge imposes coupling — is the knowledge-embodiment theorem: a maximally cohesive module embodies exactly the knowledge its class must hold. The theorem is developed in *On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule* [@loth2026cohesion], with the causal grounding in *Causal Cohesion* [@loth2026causal].
*Which language's coupling analysis surprised you? Which mechanisms did the analysis miss? Share your experience in the comments.*
**The formal development.** The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:
